planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Buttered Rum heucherella colors best with a few hours of morning sun and consistent moisture.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Buttered Rum heucherella colors best with a few hours of morning sun and consistent moisture. Large, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves emerge amber-orange in spring and deepen to rich caramel-brown through summer, with contrasting pale pink flower spikes rising above the foliage in late spring. A cross between heuchera and tiarella, it combines the bold leaf shape of tiarella with heuchera's tougher constitution and more compact, non-stoloniferous habit, making it a well-behaved clumping groundcover rather than a spreader. Use it to edge a shaded path or brighten the front of a woodland border, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Copper Frost holds its silvery overlay best out of hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Copper Frost holds its silvery overlay best out of hot afternoon sun. Deeply cut, coppery-orange leaves are brushed with a metallic silver overlay along the veins, deepening in tone through the cooler months and providing striking color contrast against greener shade companions. Airy, wiry stems carry small creamy-white flowers above the foliage in late spring, drawing in early bumblebees. Clumping and slow to spread, it holds a tidy shape for years without becoming invasive, making it a reliable choice for edging shaded beds, container plantings, or the front of a woodland border; divide only when the crown becomes congested, typically after three to four years.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Kimono heucherella is a stoloniferous spreader, unlike most clumping heucherella cultivars, and fills in as a groundcover more quickly.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Kimono heucherella is a stoloniferous spreader, unlike most clumping heucherella cultivars, and fills in as a groundcover more quickly. Deeply dissected, silver-veined leaves with a purple-red central shadow radiate outward in a lacy rosette, and short stolons root as they spread to gradually knit together a broad, textured mat. Loose spikes of small pinkish-white flowers appear above the foliage in late spring, but the finely cut, patterned leaves are the main attraction throughout the growing season. Its running habit makes it a useful, faster-filling alternative to clumping coral bells for covering bare shaded ground between shrubs or along a woodland path.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Jazz Hands foamflower wants consistent moisture and struggles in dry shade.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Jazz Hands foamflower wants consistent moisture and struggles in dry shade. Bred from native eastern foamflower stock, this Terra Nova selection carries bold, deeply cut, maple-like leaves with a dark central shadow, held on sturdy stems above which fluffy, bottlebrush spikes of small starry pink-white flowers rise in mid-spring. Its clumping, non-stoloniferous habit keeps it tidy in a mixed border rather than spreading into a running mat like straight-species foamflower, and it is a good nectar source for early native bees. Combine with hostas, ferns, and heucheras for season-long textural contrast in a shaded bed, dividing crowded clumps every three to four years in spring.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Goldband sedge is a well-behaved clumper that neither runs nor self-sows aggressively.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Goldband sedge is a well-behaved clumper that neither runs nor self-sows aggressively. Arching, grass-like leaves are edged in a bold golden-yellow band that brightens through the growing season and holds its color well into winter in mild climates, giving the evergreen clump year-round presence. It forms a neat, fountain-shaped mound that works equally well as a container centerpiece, a border edger, or massed as a groundcover under high-canopy shade trees where turf will not grow. Comb out old, tattered leaves by hand in late winter rather than shearing, and divide only when the center of the clump begins to thin.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this classic, long-cultivated variegated sedge clumps steadily without running.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this classic, long-cultivated variegated sedge clumps steadily without running. Narrow, arching, evergreen leaves are striped white along the margins in a crisper, more strongly contrasting pattern than many newer sedge cultivars, forming a dense, fountain-like tuft that holds its shape through the seasons. One of the oldest variegated Japanese sedge selections still widely grown, it is a dependable, low-maintenance edger for shaded borders and pathways and a reliable filler for mixed containers in shade. Groom out old foliage by combing with gloved fingers in late winter and divide congested clumps in spring every three to four years.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Snowline sedge is a slow, compact clumper well suited to small-scale plantings and container culture.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Snowline sedge is a slow, compact clumper well suited to small-scale plantings and container culture. This dwarf Japanese sedge forms tight, dome-shaped tufts of narrow, dark green leaves crisply edged in white, staying well under a foot tall and spreading only gradually into a neat mound. Its diminutive scale makes it ideal for the front edge of a shaded rock garden, tucked between stepping stones, or as a container and fairy-garden accent where larger sedges would overwhelm the space. It needs little maintenance beyond an occasional comb-out of old leaves and rarely requires dividing.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mackenzie sedge tolerates salt spray and coastal wind and appreciates cooler summer conditions.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Mackenzie sedge tolerates salt spray and coastal wind and appreciates cooler summer conditions. Broad, strap-like, glossy dark-green leaves form a bold, tussocky clump from which triangular flower stems rise in summer, bearing chunky, pale-brown seed heads that add coarse textural contrast to finer-leaved companions. Native to coastal cliffs and tussock grasslands of New Zealand, it is prized in maritime and Pacific Northwest gardens for its salt and wind tolerance, making it a strong choice for coastal borders, large containers, and rain gardens. It performs best where summers stay relatively cool and moist, and may struggle with prolonged heat and humidity in hot inland climates.

common_name: Oehme Palm Sedge (Ice Fountains Palm Sedge)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist to wet, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Oehme palm sedge tolerates both consistently moist soil and brief flooding, making it useful in rain gardens.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist to wet, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Oehme palm sedge tolerates both consistently moist soil and brief flooding, making it useful in rain gardens. Narrow leaves radiate from the stem tips in whorled, star-like clusters reminiscent of miniature palm fronds, an unusual texture among sedges, and this selection is edged in crisp white variegation that brightens shaded plantings all season. Named for landscape architect Wolfgang Oehme, it self-sows modestly but stays clumping rather than running, and its upright, architectural form contrasts well with broad-leaved hostas and ferns. Cut the clump back in late winter before new growth emerges to keep it looking fresh through the following season.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; shaggy shield fern is more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many Asian ferns and adapts well to typical garden soil.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; shaggy shield fern is more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many Asian ferns and adapts well to typical garden soil. New fronds unfurl a striking near-black at the emerging crosiers and stipe scales before maturing to narrow, upright, glossy dark green fronds with a strongly vertical, almost architectural habit, giving the clump a bold, semi-evergreen presence through much of winter in milder zones. Native to woodlands of China, Japan, and Korea, it is a strong textural contrast plant for a shaded border, pairing well with broader-leaved hostas and rounder ferns. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter before the new flush of dark, unfurling crosiers appears.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this crested selection of the native Christmas fern is as tough and adaptable as the species.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; this crested selection of the native Christmas fern is as tough and adaptable as the species. Leathery, evergreen fronds carry the classic stocking-shaped pinnae of the wild Christmas fern, but each frond tip and many pinnae divide into crimped, ruffled crests, giving the clump a fancier, more textured silhouette than the straight species. It shares the parent species' outstanding tolerance of dry shade, root competition, and winter cold, holding its glossy dark green fronds through snow in most of its range. Use it as a novelty accent among plainer ferns and hostas in a woodland garden, cutting only the previous year's flattened fronds back in early spring as new crosiers unfurl.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
